entries.title: After Their Playoff Loss, the Mystics Gathered for a Late-Night ‘Last Hoorah’
entries.summary: “It was just wanting to have one more moment with the same girls,” before they all dispersed for the offseason.
entries.content:
After their season came to a quiet, unsatisfying end in the first round of the playoffs Wednesday night, the Mystics lingered in the locker room.

They had gone through all of their usual postgame tasks. Head coach Sydney Johnson told them to be proud of what they had accomplished this year. They fulfilled their media obligations and showered and changed. It was soon time for the players to leave the building.

But they were not quite ready to leave each other.

So they kept the night going. Point guard Georgia Amoore volunteered her place. If this was the final day of the season for the 2026 Mystics, they would make tomorrow wait as long as it possibly could. The group all piled into Amoore’s apartment. They spent the next few hours there.

“Just a last hoorah,” forward Kiki Iriafen said. “We just hung out and talked and reminisced on the season.”

This historically young roster grew extremely close over the course of the season. Many teams speak about togetherness and love and sisterhood. Few use the aftermath of a tough playoff loss for a bittersweet last shot at a late-night hangout session. The players discussed the game they had just played, of course, because it was hard to talk about anything else at first. (The No. 4 Dream had swept the No. 5 Mystics with a pair of bruising losses.) But they soon found themselves discussing far more.

“It was really fun,” Amoore said. “First of all, let’s digest this game. But then, you know when you just get delirious, and everything’s funny, and you reflect on the randomest moments?... It was just a cute little kumbaya, to be like, Yo, let’s just let it all out.”

There is considerable focus on the future around here. Washington has a strong, young core, with a guaranteed lottery pick in the upcoming draft and plenty of salary cap space, too. This playoff loss is supposed to be only the beginning for this group. Everyone from national analysts to their own coaching staff has talked about this week as the start of something much bigger for this franchise.

But it was still an ending.

“We just have such a close group, and I feel like we really all love each other so much and love playing with each other. It was rough, just thinking, you know, Who knows what the team will look like next year?” said rookie center Lauren Betts. “It was just wanting to have one more moment with the same girls. It was such a nice little goodbye for all of us.”

Chances are high that many of those players will still be here when training camp rolls around in April. The Mystics’ only unrestricted free agent is veteran Betnijah Laney-Hamilton; a dramatic roster shakeup is unlikely. This core is expected to stay in place. But they hope they will be slightly different versions of themselves when they return to D.C.

Amoore will play this offseason in her native Australia. Much of this year was spent mentally grappling with the continued recovery from a torn ACL: Even though she had been cleared to get back on the floor months ago, she did not feel completely herself physically until fairly recently, she said. Her last offseason focused on making a return to play. This offseason will be focused on making what she calls a “Return to G.”

“I’ll have a lot of time to practice, to individually work out,” she said. “To get back to that Georgia Amoore that I’m familiar with.”

Iriafen has no plans to play elsewhere but has big plans for training and recovery: “I know that there’s another level that I can tap into and become an even better player.” Betts will play in Turkey.

Two of the Mystics’ biggest talents, Sonia Citron and Shakira Austin, will play in the Miami-based three-on-three league Unrivaled that attracts many WNBA players.

“I want to use Unrivaled to get better as a player,” said Citron, who has been an All-Star in both of her seasons with the Mystics. “Unrivaled is a great atmosphere for that. … The three-on-three setting, I think, is just really a great place to get better individually.”



Yet before they scattered for all of that offseason work, they shared the final hours of their season together. They will remember the loss. But they will remember what they did afterward, too.

“It’s having moments like that,” Amoore said. “Going into the offseason, that’s what you remember.”
entries.author: Emma Baccellieri

entries.title: Everything You Need to Know for Commanders-Colts
entries.summary: Key matchups, how to watch, pregame reading and more for Sunday’s game from London.
entries.content:
The Commanders and Colts both go into Sunday’s game in London with a 1-2 record, with Washington coming off its upset victory over the Seahawks and the Colts edging out the Texans.

Here’s everything you need to know.

Kickoff: 9:30 a.m. ET at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, London

TV: NFL Network

Betting Lines

Lines from DraftKings, as of Friday. 

Spread: Commanders +3.5

Money line: Commanders +160, Seahawks -192

Over/under: 47.5 points

Pregame Reading

Jayden Daniels traveled to London with the Commanders, leaving open the possibility in the middle part of the week that he could return just two weeks after dislocating his left elbow against the Cowboys, but the team ruled him out on Friday.

The Washington Sun’s Martenzie Johnson, who also made the trip across the pond, wrote about the team’s travel plans, which centered on achieving as much normalcy for the players as possible. Still, the 3,000-mile transatlantic flight and five-hour time difference can be a challenge even for professional football players to manage.

Backup quarterback Marcus Mariota was very effective in leading the Commanders to an upset win over the Seahawks on Sunday. Here’s how offensive coordinator David Blough played to Mariota’s strengths.

Leo Chenal was one of the Commanders’ key free agent signings this offseason as they aimed to retool their defense. He is out for the rest of the season after suffering a scary neck injury in Sunday’s game.

The Commanders re-signed a familiar face this week, bringing back Austin Ekeler, who is one of the NFL’s better all-purpose running backs.

About the Colts

Colts defensive end DeForest Buckner contemplated retirement last season after a neck injury ended his season. But he’s back, and with three sacks in as many games, he looks like the player he was before the injury.

The Colts will be without wide receiver Alec Pierce, who went on injured reserve with a heel injury this week, leaving them without one of their best deep threats.

One Big Question

Will Austin Ekeler play? 

Ekeler is one of four running backs on the Commanders’ roster and is in London with the team after being signed Monday. Coach Dan Quinn told reporters on Wednesday that Rachaad White is battling a shoulder injury, and his status for Sunday is unknown. The Commanders have struggled to get their run game going through three games, and Ekeler’s ability to affect games as a runner and a pass-catcher could give Quinn reason to play him.

But Ekeler last played for the Commanders a year ago, before a torn Achilles ended his season after two games, and that was under coordinator Kliff Kingsbury’s offense, not Blough’s.

“It’s like drinking through a fire hose trying to get everything going,” Ekeler told reporters Wednesday. “These guys have been going at it for months, and now I am here. I have been at it for two days. … I know the concepts, but it’s learning the terminology.”

Quote of the Week

“We won't put him out there before he's ready,” Quinn said of Daniels on Wednesday.

The fact that the team is being cautious with Daniels’ return makes sense given that Quinn has been criticized before for his handling of his quarterback’s health. But in his press availability this week, Daniels appeared hopeful he can be back on the field sooner than later.
entries.author: Alex Schiffer

entries.title: Capitals Beat the Hurricanes, 5-2, in Season Opener
entries.summary: Alex Tuch scored twice in his first game for Washington, while Alex Ovechkin added an assist in a win over the defending Stanley Cup champions.
entries.content:
RALEIGH, N.C. — Alex Tuch scored twice in his first game for Washington, Alex Ovechkin opened his 22nd NHL season with an assist and the Capitals beat the Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes 5-2 on Friday night.

Tuch joined the Capitals in an offseason trade after five seasons with Buffalo. The 41-year-old Ovechkin assisted on Tuch’s opening goal in Washington’s three-goal first period.

Cole Hutson, Jakob Chychrun and Ryan Leonard also scored for the Capitals, and Logan Thompson made 31 saves.

Sebastian Aho and Logan Stankoven scored for Carolina, and Brandon Bussi stopped 22 shots. The Hurricanes opened Tuesday night at home with a 1-0 overtime loss to Florida.

Tuch opened the scoring at 6:33 of the first period, beating Busso with a wrist shot. Hutson scored on a snap shot with 8:27 left in the period, and Tuch connected on a backhander with 5:37 to go.

Jakob Chychrun made it 4-0 on a power play at 1:36 of second.

Aho got one back for Carolina on a power play with 3:10 left in the second, and Leonard made it 5-1 eight seconds later. Stankoven scored midway through the third.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Tennessee's Prison Chief Will Resign After Failed Execution
entries.summary: Gov. Bill Lee announced the planned departure Saturday, after Wednesday's botched attempt to execute Christa Pike.
entries.content:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — The head of Tennessee’s prison system is resigning after the failed execution of Christa Pike, Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday.

Lee said that Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada will step down this month.

Strada said in a statement that stepping aside “is in the best interests” of the state as an independent review is carried out to determine why Pike’s execution failed Wednesday.

Pike was placed on a ventilator and remained unconscious in a hospital, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.

Hospital staff, her lawyers said, were working to save Pike’s life and as of late Thursday were trying to clear the two doses of the drug that the state uses to execute prisoners.

The stunning failure in Tennessee’s execution chamber on Wednesday has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review.

Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.

“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” they wrote in the court filing.

Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage. She later became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Trump Announces a Plan to Send $90 Checks to Millions of Medicare Recipients
entries.summary: The proposal would cost nearly $2 billion and draw from a congressionally allocated Medicare improvement funding pool.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said his administration would send nearly $100 in checks to more than 20 million adults to pay for their Medicare Part B benefits.

The plan, which would cost nearly $2 billion dollars, follows a slate of recent promises from Trump to send out individual payments to American voters in hopes of sparking voter enthusiasm for his administration ahead of the midterms. It’s unclear what authority the White House would use to go through with these plans without congressional approval.

“You will get your money almost immediately, and everything we do, we’re looking out for America’s people and America’s seniors,” Trump said in a video Saturday morning.

A fact sheet posted Saturday on the Centers for Medicaid and Medicare Services website says eligible beneficiaries will receive one $90 check or direct deposit “on or around” Oct. 8, followed by correspondence from the president in mid-October. The government’s “rebate” would cover less than half of the standard Part B monthly premium of $202.90 for those who make less than $109,000.

Not all of the estimated 64 million elderly Medicare enrollees qualify, including those on Medicare Advantage plans that route through private insurers.

“The best way to improve Medicare is to put healthcare dollars back where they belong — in the hands of our Medicare beneficiaries — and make coverage more affordable,” the CMS site says.

The president’s post late Friday announcing the plan said the checks would come from the Medicare Improvement Fund. The new fiscal year began Oct. 1, meaning the $2 billion funding pool — which Trump called a “pointless ‘Slush Fund’” — is now available for use, though it is unclear whether the White House can legally use it for rebates.

Trump’s approval ratings have hit record lows in the weeks before the midterms, especially as Americans blame the president for facing bleak economic outlooks. Following his COVID-19 era pandemic checks, Trump has repeatedly tried to revitalize his popularity by pivoting to affordability messaging and promising additional “rebates” or “dividends” — including his unpopular proposal to give $5,000 to American voters should they vote for Republicans in the midterms, a plan that could cost over $1.2 trillion.

The president doubled down on the $5,000 dividends in a two-minute video posted Saturday, saying, “I look forward to signing those checks.”

“If the Democrats win, you will have an economic depression, much like 1929. If the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pocket,” Trump said.

Trump also posted videos urging Republicans to “vote early, vote by mail or vote in-person on Election Day” to “swamp” Democrats with turnout, as well as a specific push for Pennsylvania voters.
entries.author: Marissa Martinez

entries.title: Terry McLaurin Is Likely Out for the Commanders’ London Game
entries.summary: He’ll likely join Jayden Daniels on the sidelines.
entries.content:
LONDON — Commanders receiver Terry McLaurin is unlikely to play against the Colts on Sunday in London, a source confirmed to The Washington Sun.

McLaurin was a full participant in practice on Wednesday and Thursday but showed up as limited on Friday due to a hamstring injury. He will be a game-time decision on Sunday morning.

Ben Standig was the first to report McLaurin’s condition.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

McLaurin’s absence would be a blow to Washington's offense. With starting quarterback Jayden Daniels (elbow) missing his second game in a row, the absence of the team’s number one receiver will make it slightly more difficult to move the ball and score on the Colts’ league-worst defense.

After combining for just 64 yards and zero touchdowns through the first two weeks, McLaurin got back on track last week against Seattle. He finished the game with 77 yards and an acrobatic 30-yard touchdown catch.

The passing offense will now have to lean more on receivers Stefon Diggs, Trey Burks and Antonio Williams. Tight end Chig Okonkwo will return to the lineup after missing the last two games.

McLaurin missed seven games last season due to an injured quad.
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: Trump Doxxes Tom Cotton’s Cell Phone
entries.summary: It’s all part of a unique push for permanent daylight saving time.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump posted Sen. Tom Cotton’s cell phone number to the world on Saturday, as part of a plea for his Truth Social followers to badger his Republican ally into making daylight saving time permanent.

“For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one! It should pass overwhelmingly, in a Bipartisan fashion,” Trump posted. “So, everyone in Arkansas, a State I love, and won 3 times, the last by by 34 points, tell Tom to, GET IT DONE!”

A source confirmed that the number the president shared actually belongs to Cotton. When The Washington Sun called the number minutes after Trump’s post, a recording said the mailbox was full and could not receive messages. Cotton’s office did not immediately respond to additional requests for comment.

Cotton has long detested the idea of making daylight saving time permanent. In a Senate floor speech last year, Cotton said doing so would “make winter a dark and dismal time for millions of Americans,” particularly harming kids. The Senate was only able to unanimously pass the bill in 2022 because Cotton was reportedly unaware the vote was taking place, though the measure stalled out from there.

The Arkansas Republican didn’t back down in a post on Saturday.

“Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first,” he posted on X.

Trump continued his tear against Cotton soon after.

“If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so,” he posted on Truth.

The bill, Trump wrote, “has been held up in the Senate, a place where things go to die, by Tom Cotton, for months! — And for what, other than ‘ego?’”

Trump has made a unique argument for extending daylight saving time: He believes it would be nice for golf.

“The PGA TOUR, as an example, needs more Daylight in the afternoon in order to finish their Tournaments,” Trump said in his Saturday post. “Likewise, regular Golfers, Tennis Players, Hunters and, perhaps most importantly, Farmers who want more Daylight to play or work.”

It’s unclear if the president’s additional advocacy will have much of an effect. The bill passed the House this summer, but has not moved in the Senate. Daylight saving time ends on Nov. 1. The Senate isn’t due back in D.C. until Nov. 9, after the midterm elections.

In his second post, Trump did make more of a political argument for daylight saving time.

“TAKE THE WIN TOM, JUST TAKE THE WIN! YOU NEED IT,” he wrote, “AND SO DOES OUR BELOVED REPUBLICAN PARTY!”
entries.author: Matt Berman

entries.title: Please Let Us Have a Brewers-Rays World Series
entries.summary: The baseball gods know good theater when they see it.
entries.content:
If you’re an MLB fan, and you also have a heart; if you love justice and want to see it done; if you want to see as little harm done to baseball as possible in its labor negotiations this winter, then you will invoke every lucky charm to help the Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays, Cleveland Guardians, Chicago White Sox and San Diego Padres in the MLB playoffs.

You’ll also put every hex on their trust-fund foes, the Los Angeles Dodgers, New York Yankees and even the Atlanta Braves.

What we’ve got brewing, starting with four League Division Series on Saturday, is a plot so simple, yet so powerful, that it seems to have been delivered like a sermon by the sport itself.

Go on, tell me that MLB isn’t a living thing which creates plots, then watches fans’ jaws drop as those themes play out.

Tell me that, through the generations, the game doesn’t defend its own best interests. The sport seems to sense when it is in danger and devises a narrative that leads it toward safety.

For example, for the last few years, a labor war has been brewing with Dec. 2 (when the current collective bargaining agreement runs out) as its detonation date. The central issue has been “competitive balance,” or the lack of it.

At this moment, baseball seems to be expressing its opinion on the subject. (Anthropomorphize much? Sure, why not?)

Five MLB teams have never won a World Series. Three of them are still alive and in the final eight now: the Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays and San Diego Padres.

The Brewers and Rays had the best records in their leagues. They aren’t your typical long-shot underdog modest-to-small budget teams. Both would look logical in this World Series.

In addition, over the last 125 years, two fan bases have specialized in the pain of “No Parade for You” more than anybody else. The Cleveland Guardians and Chicago White Sox have only won the World Series once each in all that time — in 1948 and 2005, respectively.

Guess who meets in the next round of the playoffs, starting Saturday? Yes, the Guardians and White Sox. One of ‘em has got to advance to the final four, even though they have the 26th and 30th lowest payrolls in MLB. Their salaries combined wouldn’t crack the top 15 payrolls.

That’s not all.

Look who else is also now guaranteed by the draw to be in that Final Four? Either the Brewers, a sensible No. 19 in payroll, representing Milwaukee, which hasn’t had a World Series winner since the Milwaukee Braves in 1957. Or San Diego, whose fans have waited in vain for all of the Padres’ 59 seasons.

Usually, the Pads are a laugh line because they’ve wasted fortunes in recent times trying to give their fans a celebration. But, with their No. 9 payroll, at least they’re making a true effort.

So, at least two of MLB’s final four teams are certain to be from our Have Not camp.

But there may be a third interloper.

The baseball gods know good theater when they see it. Right now, they’re showing off. The Rays, as usual, are toward the bottom in league payroll, estimated at under $100 million. Yet over the last 19 years, in which they have reached the playoffs 10 times and won 95 or more games six times, they have been the best illustration of how brains and scientific method, even when burdened with an old stadium, can (almost) compete evenly with filthy lucre and new magnet ballparks.

Who will the Rays’ foe be? Why, the New York Yankees, who are third in spending.

Bwahaha!

And you think Aaron Judge’s teeny tiny injury to his itsy-bitsy soleus muscle in his calf which supports his huge Return of the Mummy frame is anything but an act of baseball fate?

The harsh, real-world key to this postseason is finding somebody to beat the Dodgers (cue the Snidely Whiplash piano track) who are trying to tie Competitive Balance to the railroad tracks by winning a third straight Series.

They may.

But the toughest path to a title that any team could face is the Dodgers if they have to go through 94-win Atlanta, starting on Saturday, then 103-win Milwaukee and the 98-win Rays. The last team to have a road this tough was the Washington Nationals in 2019, against four foes that won 89, 106, 91 and 107 games.

Oh, the poor Dodgers. Gosh, they have injuries. Glorious Shohei Ohtani, in a first hint of mortality, is only able to hit, not pitch. Their pen, which “only” converted a league-average 67% of save chances, worries a fan base accustomed to sunshine on the San Gabriels every day and “we just traded for Tarik Skubal.”

The Dodgers have (honest) 14 players who are past or present All-Stars and a couple of future All-Stars, too. They are just as good as their 100 wins. But not better, no matter how short the star-struck odds that Vegas gives them.

The Brewers, Dodgers and Rays led MLB in wins. Yet Milwaukee and Tampa Bay spent $100 million less combined to get there than L.A. did.

My pick for this post-season — and, please remember my 50 years of picks have been nothing special — is the Brewers. When I fall, I fall hard. My first favorite (winning) team was the ’57 Milwaukee Braves who beat the Yankees in the World Series. I carried baseball cards of Hank Aaron and Warren Spahn in my childhood wallet. Maybe that gives me a sense of how long Milwaukee fans have waited. But anybody can feel the current Brewers’ appeal.

They are both ultra-modern in devotion to advanced metrics and scientific player development yet fundamentally old-fashioned and aesthetically pleasing in how that philosophy plays itself out in an elegantly balanced way.

The Brewers won 103 games and finished second in MLB in runs, yet only one team hit fewer home runs. The Brewers had more steals than homers. Bernie Brewer isn’t blindly worshipping the “Three True Outcomes.”

Instead, Milwaukee led MLB in batting average, that “outdated and meaningless” statistic, and were second in walks. If it were possible, the Brewers would put four men on base at once, and drive ‘em in with a gapper. All that team speed feeds an acrobatic defense.

The Miz – Jacob Misiorowski — has the best stuff I’ve ever seen, and that includes Nolan Ryan when he struck out 383 in 1973 and Sandy Koufax with 382 in 1965. I saw all of both of their primes.

Misiorowski throws as hard, or maybe slightly harder, than Ryan and has vastly better command and variety. The Miz has a cutter, slider and curveball which all move like Slimer, the Class-5 full-roaming vapor in Ghostbusters.

‘Tis said that only rich teams get to October with truly scary power aces. Not this year.

But aside from Miz, the Brewers are as obscure as they are appealing. If second baseman Brice Turang — who leads the team in WAR and could win another Platinum Glove award this year — knocked on your door and said he was running for city council, you’d probably believe him.

Winning with this cast would send a message. So would a title for the Rays, who paid for 98 wins using supermarket coupons.

If such frugality seems to prove that MLB’s competitive balance is awful, then consider that 12 NFL teams have never won a Super Bowl. There’ve been 60 of ‘em. Also, 10 NBA and 10 NHL teams have not won a title in those 60 years.

There’s no perfect apples-to-apples comparison among the major sports, but nobody has any room to brag about “balance.” MLB just catches the most flack because its owners have spent decades moaning in every labor negotiation that they don’t have socialism-for-billionaires in the form of salary caps and revenue-sharing like other sports.

MLB needs to narrow the gap between its highest and lowest spending teams. According to MLB’s own labor relations department, the top five payrolls in ’26 averaged 321 million — more than triple the average of the bottom five (93 million).

What is “sporting” about that?

MLB needs financial fixing this winter. But MLB doesn’t need to be nuked to get NFL 2.0.

If MLB is whispering anything in our ears these days, then October seems to be saying, “The game’s competitive balance” is actually better than its “financial balance.” But if you work on narrowing that economic imbalance, especially by incentivizing smaller markets to try to be competitive, you may get a dazzlingly balanced — and even more profitable — product.

If the public picks up that message, then it will put pressure on both players and owners to find a middle ground in their negotiations. Fans will say, “The game’s bent, but it’s not broke.”

Don’t erode all the progress in recent years with rules changes which have brought the time-of-game down from 3:10 in 2021 to an average of 2:39 the last four years. (In 1985, it was 2:40.)

On the other hand, if the Dodgers or Yankees win this World Series, battle lines, already drawn, will begin to march at each other.

And both sides will claim that what happens the rest of this month somehow proves their point.
entries.author: Thomas Boswell

entries.title: Ken Paxton’s Ex-Wife Says She’s Voting for Ken Paxton — Without Mentioning Ken Paxton
entries.summary: Texas state Sen. Angela Paxton’s message was paid for by a super PAC affiliated with Sen. John Thune.
entries.content:
Texas State Sen. Angela Paxton is urging Texans to vote Republican down the ballot — including for the party’s Senate nominee, who happens to be her estranged ex-husband.

“People have asked my thoughts about this election, and turns out, I have some,” she said in a 30-second spot released Saturday. “Let’s talk about the elephant in the room.”

The “elephant” is Ken Paxton, who she does not mention by name during the advertisement. The state attorney general has received criticism and snubs from some of the state’s Republican powerbrokers in the weeks leading up to the midterms, including incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, who lost to Paxton in a tight runoff in May.
https://x.com/AdImpact_Pol/status/2106409529512808548Angela Paxton, though, is staying on his side.

The state senator filed for divorce on “biblical grounds” soon after Ken Paxton launched his Senate campaign last year. The state attorney general has faced multiple scandals throughout his tenure, including his 2023 impeachment case, during which his former chief of staff testified about their alleged extramarital affair. While Angela Paxton sat through the days of testimony as a state senator, she was not allowed to cast a vote against her then-husband, though the chamber eventually acquitted him of all charges.

Angela Paxton has been privately telling donors to vote for her ex-husband in recent weeks, repeatedly referring to him as “the elephant in the room.”

She also employs another set of metaphors in the new ad, which was paid for by an affiliate arm of Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s super PAC.

“It’s not as much about the individual players on the team — it’s about getting the whole team across the finish line. Either we hold every Republican seat or we hand the future of Texas to the other team,” Paxton says. “Let’s hold the line — together.”

Thune’s Senate Leadership Fund and its affiliated branches have disclosed $130 million in Texas spending since early September, a number that will likely balloon as Nov. 3 draws closer. Much of the money has gone toward broadcast reservations and other digital advertising.
entries.author: Marissa Martinez

entries.title: Cornell President Calls Alleged Gang Rape ‘Deeply Disturbing’
entries.summary: He also committed Cornell’s support to legislative efforts to change New York’s sexual assault laws.
entries.content:
By Leah Willingham

Cornell's president called the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity house in 2024 “deeply disturbing” Saturday and said it would weigh on the university for years to come, as he pledged greater transparency amid mounting outrage over the school’s handling of the case.

In an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community, Michael Kotlikoff described the past week as one of the most difficult in the university’s history and acknowledged troubling questions about the investigations that followed the allegations.

“My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” Kotlikoff said. “It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use.”

“I believe we as an administration and we as a community must do better,” he continued.

Kotlikoff reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent investigation of the case called for by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and said Cornell’s Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also expressed support for Hochul’s decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the state attorney general.

Scrutiny has mounted in recent days over Cornell’s response to allegations that the woman was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in 2024. The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, has sued the university and seven former students.

During a student assembly hearing Thursday that gave students an opportunity to voice concerns and discuss proposals to improve Cornell’s response to sexual assault, several speakers called for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

Kotlikoff acknowledged frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough about its handling of the case, saying that has led to distrust. While citing “real legal and privacy limits” on what the university can disclose, he pledged greater transparency and more opportunities for students, parents and others to engage with university leaders.

He also committed Cornell’s support to legislative efforts to change New York’s sexual assault laws.

The case has renewed scrutiny of a New York law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving people who voluntarily consume alcohol or drugs, even if they became too intoxicated to consent.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited the law in defending his initial decision not to pursue charges, saying the woman’s original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity.

Critics have long sought to close what they call the “voluntary intoxication loophole,” which distinguishes between people incapacitated by drugs administered without their consent and those who voluntarily became intoxicated. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to the law.
entries.author: The Associated Press
